why: The statement asks for the perfect komi of Go, which in its usual reading means the standard 19x19 game. Every small-board result (5x5, rectangular boards up to 30 points, 7x7, 9x9, endgame databases at komi 0) and the Killall-Go solver answer a changed question, so they are variant. Some of them are rigorous solves of their own boards, but that does not make them a case of the 19x19 question. The 19x19 evidence is all statistical or self-play estimation from before the snapshot (Clegg 1977, the KataGo 2020 table). An estimate neither determines the value nor proves a bound on it, so these are none. The Nordic counterexample shows only that fair komi need not be an integer in an artificial position; it settles nothing about the value, so it is none and its object does not bear on the statement. The KataGo rows are generated, since the estimates themselves are KataGo output, but all of them are discarded on scope. EWS is a classical search algorithm with no learned model named, so its role is none. The 9x9 books cannot be placed after the snapshot from the record: they originate in October 2023, and the date the komi wording first appeared is unverified. Being variant, this does not matter for the outcome.
doubts: One could argue that small-board perfect komi is a 'case' of a statement that names no board size. I read the statement as standard Go, the reading the record also gives. Either way, no after-snapshot event determines a perfect komi on any board: EWS solves 5x5 at a single komi only.
